messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi is a 50-year-old animator who works from a home studio, married for twenty-two years with a fourteen-year-old son. Three years ago, his son developed a sudden, severe bacterial infection that led to sepsis and emergency surgery. Ravi spent seventy-two hours in a hospital waiting room, then another week sleeping on a vinyl recliner beside his son’s bed, the antiseptic smell so thick it clung to his clothes and hair. His son survived and is now healthy, but Ravi never left that room.

In the months afterward, Ravi noticed that certain everyday sensations would pull him back into the hospital corridor. A whiff of hand sanitizer in a grocery aisle, the chemical scent of a cleaning cart at his office, the sterile air of a dentist’s waiting room—each one made his chest tighten and his stomach drop. Medical appointments he used to take in stride became unbearable; he cancelled a routine physical three times. And sleeping alone, which he had never minded before, became its own ordeal. When his wife traveled to visit her parents, or when he stayed late in his studio to finish a deadline and crashed on the daybed, he would lie awake, alert to every creak and shift of the house, certain that something terrible was about to happen.

To manage this constant vigilance, Ravi developed what he thought of as preparation strategies. He began to revisit the weeks of his son’s illness in detail, but not simply to remember—he found himself mentally building a case against the attending surgeon, rerunning the moments when he felt the doctor had moved too slowly, and imagining what he would say if he ever confronted him. The revenge fantasy never went anywhere, but it filled the hours he could not sleep. More frequently, he rehearsed worst-case scenarios: if his son complained of a sore throat, Ravi would silently map the progression from strep to sepsis, from a cough to respiratory failure, step by step, so that nothing would catch him off guard. And he began asking his wife, every night before bed, “Are you sure he’s okay? You checked on him?” She would answer, then he would ask again ten minutes later.

The irony was that these strategies, meant to give him control, only tightened the spiral. After a long evening of replaying the surgeon’s alleged mistake, Ravi would find his senses sharpened: the faint smell of rubbing alcohol from a package delivery would set him on edge, and he would interpret a minor tension headache as the first sign of meningitis. By then, even a quiet bedroom—no smell, no procedure, only the absence of his wife’s breathing—felt unsafe, because his mind had already populated it with catastrophe. The very act of rehearsing worst cases made him more acutely aware of the hospital smell that lingered in his own jacket from a visit months ago, and more prone to notice his own pulse and interpret it as a warning.

At work, Ravi’s animation studio is in a converted warehouse; the shared break room has a faint bleach odor from the cleaning crew, and he has started taking his lunch in his car. His deadlines slip because he spends an hour each day mentally preparing for hypothetical emergencies. His wife, exhausted by the nightly reassurance loop, told him last week that she cannot keep answering the same question. That is what finally brought him in: the fear that his marriage is fraying, and the deeper terror that if his son ever falls ill again, Ravi will be too worn down by his own mind to be present. What he wants, he says, is to sleep through a single night without waking up halfway through a disaster he has already lived.
